documents.unit: AI at Carleton (Academic AI Advisory Team)
documents.title: Policies - AI at Carleton
documents.stance_why: The student-facing rule is only that 'the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves'; the page never permits or bans AI use outright, and 'faculty are encouraged to discuss this with students', so the decision on specific AI uses is left to instructors, hence delegates.
documents.summary: College-wide AI page covering employee data security rules (Gemini only for medium-risk data) and the reworded Academic Integrity policy requiring students to carry out the core intellectual substance of assignments. It does not set a permit or ban for student AI use and leaves how AI fits a course to instructors and students.

units.why: The page opens by saying existing policies carry over to AI; it is a scope statement: 'Carleton’s existing policies still apply to AI'. Coded P56 (institution-level framework) because it sets scope for the whole college.
units.anchor: Carleton’s existing policies still apply to AI

units.why: States that AI 'raise[s] novel questions around data security, attribution, and ethics', the framing principle of the college's AI policy page; an institution-level preamble, so P56.
units.anchor: AI technologies raise novel questions around data security, attribution, and ethics

units.why: Employees 'should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools'; a privacy rule for staff and faculty, so P50 (protect data), actor all because it binds all employees, modality should-not, restricting.
units.anchor: Carleton employees should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools

units.why: Names Google Gemini as 'the one exception' to the ban on entering data into ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity; a preference for a vetted tool under the Google agreement, so P50 rather than P65 because it is a user rule, not a contract review.
units.anchor: The one exception is Google Gemini, which may be used as described below

units.why: Community members 'are welcome to submit low and medium risk data' into Gemini when logged in with Carleton accounts, because of the Google agreement; permission within a vetted tool, P50, modality may.
units.anchor: welcome to submit low and medium risk data
units.policy: Carleton community members may submit low and medium risk data into Gemini when logged in through their Carleton accounts.

units.why: 'Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data' with Gemini; a data-protection prohibition, P50, modality should-not (the text uses 'should').
units.anchor: Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data

units.why: People should 'contact infosec@carleton.edu' before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors including other generative AI tools; a data-protection procedure favouring vetted tools, P50, modality should.
units.anchor: Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors, including other generative AI tools
units.policy: Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors, including other generative AI tools, contact infosec@carleton.edu.

units.why: Reports that the Academic Integrity policy was reworded 'to better articulate the guidelines around AI use in students’ academic work'; this is an institutional framework fact (P56), not itself a rule, so informs.
units.anchor: reworded its Academic Integrity policy to better articulate the guidelines around AI use

units.why: The crucial phrase says students are expected to complete assignments so 'the core intellectual substance' is carried out by the student; the student must remain the one doing the central thinking, so P32 (primary problem-solver) rather than P19, since it does not name AI generation outright.
units.anchor: students are expected to complete all assignments
units.policy: Students are expected to complete all assignments in a manner ensuring that the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves.

units.why: 'the responsibility lies with each student to ensure that they identify and complete the core intellectual substance'; students own the judgement of what must be their own work, P29, modality must.
units.anchor: the responsibility lies with each student to ensure that they identify and complete

units.why: 'faculty are encouraged to discuss this with students' including how AI might 'assist or hinder' learning; a recommendation to instructors to talk with students about expectations. No type covers instructor-student discussion of AI expectations (P09 is a syllabus statement, P57 is about suspected misuse), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to discuss this with students, both generally and with regards to AI
units.uncovered_note: Instructors are encouraged to discuss with students, in general and about AI, what the course work is for and how AI might help or hinder learning.

documents.unit: Writing Across the Curriculum (Working with AI, resources for faculty)
documents.title: AI Course Policies
documents.stance_why: The page tells faculty that 'those decisions are ultimately up to you' and points to 'templates for policies that ban almost all AI use, allow some AI use, and allow all AI use', so it sets no stance itself and hands the choice to instructors.
tiers: templates: ban almost all AI use
documents.summary: Writing Across the Curriculum guidance to faculty on writing course AI policies, with a framework of questions and advice to explain rationale and keep dialogue. It sets no common rule and points to ban, some-use and all-use templates.

units.why: Advises instructors to 'start with a working knowledge of what current AI tools can do' before setting policy; this is learning about AI before deciding, P63 (support faculty in learning AI), modality should.
units.anchor: Start with a working knowledge of what current AI tools can do

units.why: The page describes 'basic techniques for running your assignment through generative AI tools like ChatGPT' so instructors see how uses help or hinder learning; faculty learning about AI before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: techniques for running your assignment through generative AI tools like ChatGPT

units.why: Tells instructors to 'seriously consider what writing tasks you want students to do themselves' versus with AI; the decision about permitted AI is the instructor's, so P04.
units.anchor: Seriously consider what writing tasks you want students to do themselves

units.why: Says a blanket ban is 'not a practical — or even particularly desirable — solution' because nearly everyone uses AI-based spell and grammar checks; advice against a blanket ban, coded P04 (rule set by instructor in finer-grained way) as no type covers advice against bans.
units.anchor: that’s not a practical — or even particularly desirable — solution

units.why: Notes that AI can help students focus by easing 'ancillary tasks ... (grammar, citations, proofreading, etc.)'; writing-support uses that instructors may allow, so P18 (prose AI treated separately from code), informs.
units.anchor: some applications of AI can actually help them focus on the most important aspects

units.why: Says it is 'reasonable to allow, or even to explicitly require' some AI techniques in some assignments; permission or requirement set per assignment, coded P02 (permit or encourage) with modality may, rather than P04 since the passage speaks to what is allowed.
units.anchor: it would be reasonable to allow, or even to

units.why: 'those decisions are ultimately up to you': the instructor decides which skills students practise unassisted; P04.
units.anchor: those decisions are ultimately up to you

units.why: Advises instructors to 'explain the rationale behind' their AI guidelines and to 'focus on learning and intellectual growth'. No type covers instructors explaining the reasons to students (P41 is the rationale itself), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: explain the rationale behind them
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should explain to students the rationale behind their AI rules, with focus on learning rather than punishment.

units.why: 'State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus': an instruction to put AI expectations in the syllabus, P09, modality should (advisory page).
units.anchor: State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus

units.why: Says best syllabus statements are 'clear, concise, and explanatory rather than punitive'; guidance on the form of the syllabus AI statement, so P09.
units.anchor: the best syllabus statements are clear, concise, and explanatory rather than punitive

units.why: Lists what 'a complete policy would address' (permitted uses, forbidden uses, documentation, variation, rationale); syllabus content requirements, P09, modality should.
units.anchor: a complete policy would address
units.policy: A complete AI policy addresses how students may use AI, what uses are forbidden, how use is documented or disclosed, whether rules vary by assignment, and the overall rationale.

units.why: Asks 'how do you want students to document, cite, or otherwise disclose' AI use when it is allowed; the instructor should set a disclosure rule, so P24 with modality should.
units.anchor: how do you want students to document, cite, or otherwise disclose

units.why: Says the AI rules may differ by assignment and 'you’ll also need to write clear AI policies for any assignment that deviates'; assignment-level rules, P04, modality must (need to).
units.anchor: you’ll also need to write clear AI policies for any assignment that deviates

units.why: 'It’s okay to be a bit general' in the syllabus statement; permission to keep the syllabus statement general, part of the syllabus-content guidance, P09, modality may.
units.anchor: It’s okay to be a bit general when you frame these ideas

units.why: 'it’s probably best practice to include a more specific version of your AI policy as part of the prompt for every major writing assignment'; AI statement in assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: include a more specific version of your AI policy as part of the prompt

units.why: 'be prepared to spend some time discussing them in class' by the first major writing assignment; classroom discussion of the AI rules is not covered by any type (P09 is written statements), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: be prepared to spend some time discussing them in class
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should discuss their AI policies in class, no later than the first major writing assignment, explaining the logic and inviting questions.

units.why: Says it is 'virtually impossible to prove' AI use 'conclusively' even when detected; an enforcement-limit statement. P39 (do not rely on detectors) fits because it says AI use cannot be reliably proved, though no detector is named; informs.
units.anchor: it’s virtually impossible to prove this conclusively

units.why: 'those prohibitions may also be unenforceable in practice' and 'we will increasingly need to trust our students to follow our policies voluntarily'; staff rely on student responsibility rather than policing, P60, modality should.
units.anchor: we will increasingly need to trust our students to follow our policies voluntarily

units.why: Advises instructors to 'create as open a dialogue as possible' so students feel comfortable 'coming to you with questions about the use of AI'; students asking the instructor, P10.
units.anchor: students feel comfortable coming to you with questions about the use of AI

units.why: Tells instructors to explain how AI 'would diminish students’ learning or undermine the benefits' of the assignments; a learning rationale (AI shortcuts the practice), P41, modality informs.
units.anchor: using AI to generate text or perfect their grammar diminish students’ learning

units.why: Instructors should tell students 'what limitations of AI tools' they should know, such as unreliable information; students are told to watch AI output quality, P31, modality should.
units.anchor: What limitations of AI tools should they be aware of

units.why: Instructors should address 'what should students do if they’re unsure about a particular use of AI' and 'when and how should they ask you'; P10 (ask before using), modality should.
units.anchor: What should students do if they’re unsure about a particular use of AI

units.why: 'encourage them to ask questions, especially about applications of AI tools that aren’t explicitly covered' by the policy; students asking when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: encourage them to ask questions, especially about applications of AI tools that aren’t explicitly covered

units.why: Links 'templates for policies that ban almost all AI use, allow some AI use, and allow all AI use'; named templates of three levels, P05, informs; the page itself delegates.
units.anchor: Templates for policies that ban almost all AI use, allow some AI use

notes: Only two university-layer documents were included; no school or computing documents. Three units were UNCOVERED, all about instructors discussing or explaining AI rules to students.
